newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Ascom H1 profit up, sees bright 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ascom H1 profit up, sees bright 1996.

text.p: Swiss telecommunications group Ascom Holding AG on Tuesday posted a 39 percent jump in first half operating profit and forecast higher operating results for the full year.
But the company said 1996 net profit would depend on the search for a partner for its troubled U.S.-based unit Timeplex.
While Ascom has benefitted from recent streamlining, it continues to be plagued by past legacies and said it had slashed 270 jobs at Timeplex while searching for a partner or buyer.

Ascom's operating profit rose to 39 million Swiss francs ($31.44 million) in the first half from 28 million last year as the operating margin rose to 2.7 percent from 2.0 percent in first half 1995 due to ongoing cost-cutting efforts.
"Given unchanged market conditions, fiscal 1996 is expected to close with an improved year-on-year operating result," Ascom's chairman Felix Wittlin told a news conference.
"Group net profit will depend on the search for a partner (for Timeplex)," he added, noting that this could lead to restructuring costs or provisions.
First half sales were roughly stable at 1.4 billion francs.
New orders were up three percent to 1.51 billion, helped by a strong telecommunications segment that gained from investment in digital telephone equipment by state-owned PTTs ahead of privatisation.
The telecommunications segment also won a promising contract to provide mobile public telephones for Mexico, a product that Ascom looks to with much promise in developing countries.
Chief financial officer Jakob Schlapbach said Ascom's debt had fallen by 96 million francs to 580 million by mid-1996, a big improvement from debt of one billion at the end of 1994.
"Interest payments on our debt are no longer our main problem," Wittlin told reporters.

Ascom, the product of a 1987 merger of three traditional suppliers to the Swiss PTT, ran into serious difficulties in 1992 but has gradually pulled itself out of the danger zone by focusing on core activities and selling off the rest.
The process of restoring Ascom to full health, however, is not complete and during the first half it sold off small companies with combined sales of some 100 million francs.
Chief executive Hans-Ulrich Schroeder, who took over last July, shook up corporate culture at Ascom in a bid to ensure that managers follow budgets and strive to beat competitors.
Almost 10 years after its birth, Ascom is also still consolidating its operations in European countries and doing away with superfluous management levels.
But while Ascom's telecommunications and service automation segments are meeting expectations, the enterprise networks segment that mainly comprises Timeplex still causes headaches.
In the first half, telecommunications posted a 34 percent rise in operating profit to 79 million Swiss francs and the service automation segment rose 66 percent to 10 million.

But enterprise networks saw losses widen by 117 percent to 39 million Swiss francs. Timeplex, bought by Ascom in 1991, supplies products and services to private telecommunications networks worldwide for many blue-chip companies.
Promising talks with a potential partner for Timeplex broke down this summer when the unnamed suitor ran into profitability problems.

Talks with other companies are now under way, but Ascom decided in August it could not wait and initiated sweeping restructuring measures that included installing new top management and cutting one-fifth of Timeplex workforce.
($1=1.2403 Swiss Franc)
